title: 1dfuonm
The Disagreement over Mut'a Marriage (Temporary Marriage)
hook: How did a word of a verse and a practice in the Prophet's time open into two readings of jurisprudence?
scenes.0.text: Surah Nisâ, verse 24, lists the women who are lawful to marry, and then says, "Give the women you have enjoyed their dowries as an obligation". The word "istemte'tum" in the verse means "you have used", and it comes from the same root as mut'a. In the Qur'an, this word refers to a marriage for a certain period of time, or mut'a. The same word is understood to mean marriage and dowry in Sunni reading. The language of the verse is clear for both readings. The Jafari school, on the other hand, sees this root meaning of the word and the emphasis of the verse "mahir" as the basis in the Qur'an for marriage with a fixed duration.
scenes.1.text: In his commentary on Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Ubay b. It is reported that some Sahaba, such as Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud, recited this verse with the addition of the phrase "until an appointed time". This appendix is not from the text of the Qur'an, but it shows how the Sahaba understood the verse. The Jafari school also continues to read the 24th of Nisan as a marriage with a fixed duration. There are three conditions for this marriage: time, mahr and iddah. The time is fixed and the dowry is determined. And when the period is over, the marriage is dissolved of its own accord, and the wife waits. So mut'a is not a secret affair, it's a marriage with rules.
scenes.2.text: Mut'a was used during the time of the Prophet, especially on expeditions. According to the story of Jabir bin Abdullah, one day the Prophet's spokesman came and announced that the marriage was allowed. Jabir relates that the practice continued during the caliphate of Abu Bakr after the Prophet and during the early times of the caliphate of Umar. The Jafari school is based on this early practice and maintains a fixed-term marriage in the same manner. Jabir's word is important because it was given on the day of the Prophet. And the ban only started to be talked about later.
scenes.3.text: The rumors about the ban don't add up. In one tradition, Ali tells Ibn Abbas that the Prophet forbade mut'a and the meat of domestic donkeys on the day of Khaybar. According to the Muslim tradition in 1406, mut'a was allowed in the year of the conquest of Mecca, after which it was said, "Allah has made it unlawful until the Day of Judgment". Other stories link the ban to the Battle of Evtas or the Hajj of Veda. So there's a clear discrepancy between the rumors about the history of the ban. In the face of this chaos, the Jafari school takes the permission given during the time of the Prophet and maintains the marriage for a certain period.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: 19izoul
The Prophet
scenes.4.text: Sources relate a speech by Caliph Umar. Umar says in this speech that he forbids two mut'ahs and that he will punish the perpetrator. One of them is the marriage of women during the hajj. Some of the similarities of the narrative include the phrase, "Both were in the time of the Prophet". The Jafari school continues mut'ah with women according to the practice of the Prophet before this speech. For him, the forbidden word is the word of a caliph, while the permission is for the Prophet's own days. The word of the Caliph does not invalidate the permission given by the Prophet.
scenes.4.art.actors.0.label: 1nai5fq
Caliph Umar
scenes.5.text: It is attributed to '**Ali**: "If Umar had not forbidden, only a miserable person would have resorted to adultery". A similar statement is also found in Ibn Abbas and Atha's Musannef and Taberi commentary by Abdurrezzak. Whether it's Ali or Ibn Abbas and his health is debatable. But the word tells us that the mut'ah is seen as a legitimate way to protect people from the haram. The Jafari school maintains the mut'a with the permission of the Prophet. Those who desire marriage should observe the prescribed period and the prescribed mahr. Without these conditions, two adults cannot enter into this marriage.
scenes.5.art.actors.0.label: lhg99z
Imam Ali
scenes.6.text: Ibn Abbas is reported to have authorized the mut'ah. It is also reported that he linked this fatwa to conditions such as compulsion and the minority of women. The news that he later abandoned that view completely comes with weak bonds. Ibn Hajar mentions this in Fethu'l-Barī. In short, a mut'a is a temporary marriage between two adults, with a fixed duration and dowry. There is no divorce. When the marriage period is over, the marriage is dissolved and the wife has a waiting period. The sources don't describe it as a secret deception. The Jafari reading of Nisan 24 is a marriage of fixed duration, while the Sunni reading is a marriage of ordinary and dowry. In Muslim 1405d, Jabir says that the practice continued during the time of the Prophet and Abu Bakr, and that Umar forbade it. In Muslim 1406a, Sebre tells that they were allowed, then told to let go. Buhari in 4216 Hz. Ali informs Ibn Abbas of the ban on the day of Khaybar. It depends on the rumors about the ban and the day it came out. Nevevi says there is a community on this, but the Cafer school does not accept this community. Most Sunni sects today do not consider mut'ah to be halal. The Jaffari school, on the other hand, maintains it on the condition of time, period and deadline. The Kafirs accept mut'ah as permissible because they think that those who believe that the Prophet brought a Halal, unjustly caliphate cannot make it haraam.
sunni.0.says: At the battle of Khaybar the Prophet forbade mut'a and the meat of domestic donkeys; Imam Ali reports this to Ibn Abbas.
sunni.1.says: Ibn Abbas allows mut'ah, his student says it depends on difficult conditions, such as the lack of women. Secondary transmission.
sunni.2.says: Permission is given in the year of the conquest; then it is said, "God has made this forbidden until the Day of Resurrection." Narration of Sabra b. Ma'bad. 1406a: in the permitted mut'a, the Prophet saying, "Whoever has such a woman in hand, let him leave her."
sunni.3.says: The Prophet's herald comes and announces that permission to benefit has been given.
sunni.4.says: Hajj mut'a and women mut'a; Caliph Umar says he forbids both and will punish them.
sunni.5.says: The narration saying "Mut'a was at the beginning of Islam"; it is said to have become forbidden by verse 23:6.
sunni.5.grade: Ali al-Za'i: weak; Ibn Hajar: weak and shadh, the chain is broken
sunni.6.says: An evaluation of the mut'a narrations and of the narrations of Ibn Abbas's retraction.
sunni.7.says: The Nawawi states that it is forbidden after the mut'ah, and it is forbidden by the Ummah.
shia.0.says: The conditions of mut'a: a fixed term, a fixed dowry; the woman's iddah.
shia.1.says: The rulings and narrations on mut'a.
shia.2.says: A compilation gathering Shia narrations, in all of whose chapter titles the term "mut'a" appears.
shia.3.says: The Imamiyya claim of consensus on the permissibility of mut'a, and its evidence.
shia.4.says: The narration of the reading "ila ajalin musamma" in 4:24 from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud and others.
shia.4.grade: SECONDARY: from a partisan article; primary text not seen
disputes.0.title: ro6d2
What does "istemte'tum" and Nisâ 4:24 mean?
disputes.0.shia: The word "istemte'tum" in Nisâ 4:24 is read together with the dowry in both traditions. The Ja'fari reading takes it as a marriage of fixed duration; the "specified term" reading is also used as support for this meaning.
disputes.0.sunni: The word "istemte'tum" at Exodus 4:24 is read with the mehir in both traditions. In the Sunni reading, the word is the use of the common marriage; additional readings do not count as the Qur'anic text; Mu'minun 23:6 draws the line as marriage and the handmaid.
disputes.1.title: 7zv7ci
Was the permission lifted?
disputes.1.shia: That permission for mut'a was given in the Prophet's time is mentioned in both sources. The Ja'fari school ties the prohibition to Caliph Umar's statement and does not accept that the verse and the Prophet's permission were lifted by it.
disputes.1.sunni: That permission for mut'a was given in the Prophet's time is mentioned in both sources. In the Sunni account, the permission is regarded as abrogated by the narrations of Khaybar, the Conquest, Awtas and the Farewell Pilgrimage (Bukhari 5115, Muslim 1406); there is a difference in the date, and in the end the ruling of prohibition is adopted.
disputes.2.title: g0tmev
To whom is Caliph Umar's prohibition attributed?
disputes.2.shia: Caliph Umar's speech forbidding the two mut'as also appears in Muslim. The Ja'fari reading ties the prohibition to his own statement and takes the permission of the Prophet's time as the basis.
disputes.2.sunni: Caliph Umar's speech forbidding the two mut'as also appears in Muslim. In the Sunni account, he reminded people of the prohibition the Prophet had set and enforced it; in some narrations, the knowledge of the prohibition reached him later.
questions.0: Muslim 1217 relates that Caliph Umar forbade the two mut'as. The sentence "It existed in the Prophet's time" appears in the parallels of the narration. How does this account make you think about the period to which the prohibition is tied?
questions.1: The date of the prohibition is told differently as Khaybar, the Conquest, Awtas and the Farewell Pilgrimage. What does this difference in date make you attend to when reading abrogation narrations?
questions.2: Jabir relates that the practice continued into the time of Caliph Abu Bakr and the early period of Caliph Umar (Muslim 1405). How does such a long continuation of the early practice shape how one reads the history of jurisprudence?
questions.3: The narration that ties Ibn Abbas's fatwa to hardship and the narration that says he retracted stand side by side. How does one look at the chains to understand the final form of a Companion's fatwa?
questions.4: The source and chain of the saying "Had Caliph Umar not forbidden it" are disputed. What weight does a saying whose chain is not clear carry on the subject of mut'a?
summary: Mut'a is also mentioned in Sunni books as a marriage practiced during the time of the Prophet. And if you are a disbeliever, then you are a disbeliever. In Sunni sects, it's considered haram with the following prohibitions.
key: Mut'a: it existed in the Prophet's time
notes.0: Mut'a is a marriage for a term and is associated with Nisâ 4:24.
notes.1: That it was practiced on expeditions in the Prophet's time appears in the sources of both schools.
notes.2: It is reported in Sunni sources that it was later forbidden (dates such as Khaybar, the conquest of Mecca).
notes.3: Caliph Umar's speech of prohibition appears in Muslim 1217.
notes.4: In Ja'fari jurisprudence it continues with conditions. It is regarded as forbidden in the four Sunni schools; what is common is that it was practiced in the Prophet's time.
